subject: Culture
title: Space Burials
description: A fast breakdown of Space Burials for builders.

hook.text: Gene Roddenberry, creator of Star Trek, had his ashes launched into space in 1997. Tickets now start at $2,500.

buildup.text: Companies like Celestis and Elysium Space offer to send cremated remains into orbit, to the moon, or into deep space.

discovery.text: Clyde Tombaugh, who found Pluto, has ashes aboard New Horizons—the farthest human remains from Earth.

twist.text: Native Hawaiians protested lunar burials on Mauna Kea's telescopes. Sacred space on Earth extends to sacred space above.

climax.text: Space burial turns the cosmos into a cemetery. It extends humanity's need to be remembered beyond the planet itself.

punchline.text: We send our dead to the stars because we've always looked up.

quiz.question: Whose ashes are aboard the New Horizons spacecraft?

details.summary: Space burials launch cremated remains into orbit, to the moon, or into deep space — the ultimate frontier funeral. Companies like Celestis and Elysium Space offer this service, with prices starting at a few thousand dollars. Gene Roddenberry and Timothy Leary are among those buried in space.
details.whyItMatters: Space burial represents humanity's newest death ritual, extending our relationship with mortality beyond Earth. It raises questions about space debris, indigenous sacred sites on the moon, and access inequality.
takeaways: Space burial launches cremated remains into orbit or beyond
Prices range from $2,500 for suborbital flights to $12,500 for the moon
Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry's ashes were launched into orbit

faq.question: How does space burial work?
faq.answer: A small portion of cremated remains (typically 1-7 grams) is placed in a capsule and launched on a commercial rocket. Options include suborbital flights (remains briefly reach space then return), orbital flights (remains circle Earth before re-entering), lunar missions, and deep space voyages.

faq.question: Is space burial controversial?
faq.answer: Yes. Native Hawaiian groups have protested lunar burial missions, arguing the moon is a sacred ancestor (Hina). Space debris concerns make orbital burials problematic. Environmental groups question the carbon footprint of rocket launches for memorial purposes.
